lede: Some metals fizz the moment they touch water; others sit in a drawer for years and never change. The difference is how readily a metal gives its outer electrons away, and putting the metals in that order lets you predict every reaction in this topic instead of guessing.
can: Write the eight metals of the reactivity series in order, potassium down to copper.
Say what each metal does with air, with cold water and with steam, and name the products.
Explain the whole series in one sentence, using the words positive ion.

text: The reactivity series: air, water and steam

md: Drop a lump of calcium into water and it fizzes straight away. A copper coin can sit in a puddle for years and stay a coin. Metals differ in how readily they react, and chemists line them up in one fixed order — the reactivity series — so the differences can be predicted instead of guessed.

explain: Potassium. Top means most reactive, and the order runs downwards to copper at the bottom.

text: 1. Reactivity means letting go of electrons

md: When a metal reacts it hands over the electrons in its outer shell and becomes a **positive ion**. Magnesium gives away two: $\ce{Mg -> Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$. So the order of the series is simply how willingly each metal does that — **reactivity is the tendency of a metal to form its positive ion**.

title: Why potassium beats calcium
md: A potassium atom has one outer electron to give away; a calcium atom has two, and it holds them a little more tightly. Potassium parts with its single electron more easily, so it forms its positive ion more readily and reacts harder with the same water.

prompt: Reactivity is the tendency of a metal to form its ______ ion.
explain: Positive. Metals lose electrons, and losing negative charge leaves a positive ion behind.

md: Heat any of these metals strongly in air and it joins with oxygen to make the **metal oxide**. What tells them apart is what you see while it happens. **Iron** throws **orange sparks**. **Magnesium** burns with a **bright white light** and leaves a white solid. **Copper** never flames: it **glows red**, and a black solid is left. Learn the three sights as well as the products, because the sight is what a question hands you.

prompt: A metal is heated strongly in air and glows red without sparking. Which metal is it?
explain: Copper glows red and leaves black copper(II) oxide. Iron sparks orange; magnesium gives the bright white light.

md:
Only the top three — potassium, sodium and calcium — react with **cold water**, and they give the **metal hydroxide** and **hydrogen**:
calcium + water → calcium hydroxide + hydrogen, or $\ce{Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2}$.
Watch a granule of calcium and there are five things to say: bubbles of gas; the granule sinking and rising as the bubbles lift it; the calcium slowly disappearing; a **colourless** solution with a white solid in it; and the beaker warming up.

explain: Hydroxide. Cold water always gives the hydroxide; hold on to that, because steam is about to give something different.

md:
**The question.** Magnesium is heated in a stream of steam. Complete the word equation, and say what the damp mineral wool is for.
**Step 1 — decide which water you are in.** Steam is water in the gas state and it is far hotter, so the products are not the cold-water ones. Magnesium does not react with cold water at all.
**Step 2 — write the products.** Steam gives the metal **oxide** and hydrogen, so: magnesium + steam → magnesium oxide + hydrogen.

prompt: Finish step 2: zinc + steam → zinc ______ + hydrogen
explain: Oxide. Every metal that reacts with steam gives its oxide and hydrogen, so zinc behaves exactly as magnesium did.

md:
**Step 3 — the mineral wool.** It is damp on purpose. Heating it boils the water it is soaked in, and that steam travels down the tube to the magnesium. Its job is to **supply the steam**, not to soak up heat.
**Step 4 — read off the observations.** Inside the tube you would see a bright white light, and a white solid left where the ribbon had been.

prompt: So what is the damp mineral wool for?
options: heating it boils the water in it, which supplies the steam
it absorbs the heat so the tube does not crack
it dries the hydrogen before it is collected
answer: heating it boils the water in it, which supplies the steam
explain: It is the steam generator. Drying the gas is a different job done by a different chemical, and nothing here needs a heat shield.

md: Every reaction here makes **hydrogen**, and a question will ask how it is collected. It is collected **over water**, because hydrogen is **insoluble**: it bubbles up, pushes the water out of the tube and stays there. To test it, hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube — hydrogen burns with a **squeaky pop**.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "The Reactivity Series"
why: See the three groups of metals run past in order: cold water, steam, and nothing at all.

prompt: Why can hydrogen be collected over water?
options: it burns with a squeaky pop
explain: Because it does not dissolve, it survives the journey up through the water. Being lighter than air is why upward delivery also works, and the pop is the test, not the reason.

Observations must be fully qualified: *colourless solution*, not *clear*; *heat given out*, not *heat*. Never write back an observation the stem has already handed you.
